title: Epiphany: the light spreads
hookLine: the magi, the baptism, the wedding at Cana: God shown to the world

cards: Strangers arrive in a small town. They've come a long way, from somewhere east. Matthew calls them wise men; they read the sky, and they say a star has led them here.
In the King James: "for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him." They find a house in Bethlehem, a young mother and a child.
And these foreigners kneel on the floor and open their treasures: gold, frankincense and myrrh. In Matthew's Gospel, the ones who come to worship the child are outsiders from far away.
Today's word is the feast that tells their story, and keeps going.

teach.b: Epiphany, from the Greek epiphaneia: an appearing, a showing. It falls on the sixth of January, the day after the twelve days end, and it's one idea told in three stories: God shown to the world.

teach.h: THE MAGI, THE RIVER, THE WEDDING.
teach.b: First, the magi: the light reaching people from far away. Western churches put the wise men at the center of the day. Second, the baptism of Jesus in the Jordan, when a voice from heaven calls him beloved.

Orthodox churches call the feast Theophany, God shown, and center it there. Priests bless the waters, and in some places they throw a cross into a cold river or the sea, and swimmers dive in after it.

Third, a wedding at Cana, where Jesus turns water into wine. John writes: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory." The thread through all three is who gets to see.

teach.h: THE GENTILES SHALL COME TO THY LIGHT.
teach.b: Isaiah had said, "And the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising." Gentiles means the nations, everyone who wasn't Jewish.
So Epiphany is the season when Christians say the light spreads outward, to everybody. In Spain and parts of Latin America, Three Kings Day is when children get their presents.
Some families chalk the year and the letters C, M and B above their front door, a blessing for the house.
And in everyday English, an epiphany is a sudden moment when something becomes clear, a sense borrowed from this feast.

how: Western churches celebrate Epiphany on January 6 with the story of the magi, and some families bless their doors with chalk; Orthodox churches keep Theophany, remembering Christ's baptism with the blessing of the waters.

a yearly blessing of the farm animals
a feast of God shown to the whole world

games.q: you're one of the magi. you've followed a star a long way, and it leads not to a palace but to an ordinary house and a small child. what do you do?
o: decide you've got the wrong place and leave.
ask to see the king in charge.
games.why: they fall down and worship him, and give gold, frankincense and myrrh. the outsiders see it.

practice: Think back over the last day for a moment when something became clear: a person you saw differently, a problem that suddenly made sense, something beautiful you almost walked past. Let it come back, and look at it again.
If you pray, give thanks for what was shown; if you don't, just notice that seeing happened.

wordCard.voice: Epiphany. From the Greek for a showing. The feast on January 6, when Christians remember God shown to the whole world. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an appearing, a showing forth. used of a god's appearance or a ruler's arrival.

carryVoice: Your line: the light is for everyone. Sixteen weeks on the path, day one hundred twelve.
